\begin{example}{Example}{The power-series safety margin revisited.}{ex-m-test-power}%
If \(\sum c_n(x-a)^n\) has radius \(R>0\), fix \(0<r<R\). On \(|x-a|\le r\), take \(M_n=|c_n|r^n\). This numerical series converges because \(r\) lies inside the radius. The M-test proves uniform convergence on that smaller interval. An endpoint at distance \(R\) requires its own analysis.%
\end{example}
\begin{warning}{Warning}{Uniform convergence does not control every operation.}{warn-m-test-derivatives}%
The series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n^2x)/n^2\) passes the M-test on \(\mathbb R\). But its formally differentiated series is \(\sum\cos(n^2x)\), which diverges at \(x=0\) because its terms equal \(1\). The original M-test does not justify that differentiation.%
\end{warning}
The M-test is sufficient, not necessary. A function series with constant terms \(f_n(x)=(-1)^{n-1}/n\) converges uniformly on any set, because the alternating-series remainder is at most \(1/(N+1)\) independently of \(x\). But any nonnegative majorant \(M_n\) must be at least \(1/n\), so no convergent majorant exists.%
